provenance.method: Practical discovery question assembled from reviewed England NHS/NICE routes and claimless Resources. Expanded on 2026-09-03 to cover referral, waiting, Right to Choose, outcome and private-assessment boundaries without making a personalised diagnostic inference.

question: How do I start looking into an adult autism assessment in England?
why_it_matters: Online screening, self-identification, local NHS referral, England Right to Choose, private assessment and formal diagnosis are different routes and can easily be blurred together.
current_understanding: The NHS says a GP can explain the local route and can often refer adults to an autism team. Adult assessment may include questionnaires, developmental history, information from someone who knew the person earlier in life where available, current-life information and other records. Waiting can take months or longer. In England, NHS Right to Choose may allow a person to choose another NHS assessment service; this is an NHS choice route and is not the same thing as simply paying privately. If the assessment concludes that the person is not autistic or they disagree with the result, the NHS describes asking the GP or assessment team about another team/second opinion. Local eligibility, waiting times, pre-assessment support and acceptance/follow-up of independent reports still vary. ND Oracle does not interpret a screening score as diagnosis or decide whether assessment is the right choice for an individual.
evidence_needed: Current local ICB/provider pathway, waiting-time and pre/post-assessment support evidence across England, kept separate from the national NHS/NICE route.
reopening_conditions: NHS England, NHS public guidance or NICE materially changes adult autism assessment guidance.
England Right to Choose rules materially change.
A national referral or commissioning rule changes.
dissent: Formal diagnosis can be useful for some people and unnecessary, inaccessible or unwanted for others; ND Oracle should not treat either seeking or not seeking diagnosis as inherently superior.
